primary.key: The Master said, ‘My praying has been for a long time.’
primary.s: Gravely ill, asked by Tsze-lu for leave to pray, the Master replies; Zhu Xi, on 7.34, reads it as an indirect refusal: prayer is repentance and amendment to seek the spirits’ help, and a sage whose conduct accorded with them had nothing to repent.
primary.src: Zhu Xi, Lunyu jizhu, on 7.34, zh.wikisource (Sishu zhangju jizhu, juan 4), revision 2285801 (2023)

basis.words: 禱者，悔過遷善，以祈神之佑也。…聖人未嘗有過，無善可遷。其素行固已合於神明，故曰：「丘之禱久矣。」…故孔子之於子路，不直拒之，而但告以無所事禱之意。
basis.gloss: Praying is repenting of faults and moving to the good, so as to ask the protection of the spirits. … The sage never had a fault and had no good to move to; his constant conduct already accorded with the spirits, so he said, ‘My praying has been for a long time.’ … So Confucius did not refuse Tsze-lu outright, but only told him that there was no call to pray.

standby.key: ‘Let relaxation and enjoyment be found in the polite arts.’
standby.s: After maxims on the will, on virtue and on perfect virtue, the chapter turns to recreation; He Yan, on 7.6, explains its word for relaxation, literally ranging, by the six arts being not enough to lean on, as virtue and perfect virtue are.
standby.src: He Yan, Lunyu jijie, on 7.6, zh.wikisource (the Jijie notes in Lunyu zhushu, juan 7), revision 2268335 (2023)

basis.words: 據，杖也。德有成形，故可據。…依，倚也。仁者功施於人，故可倚。…藝，六藝也，不足據依，故曰遊。
basis.gloss: [On the line on virtue:] ‘grasp’ is to lean on as on a staff; virtue has a settled form, so it can be leaned on. … [On the line on perfect virtue:] ‘accord with’ is to rest against; the work of humaneness reaches others, so it can be rested on. … The arts are the six arts; they are not enough to lean or rest on, so the text says ‘range’ (遊). (Untagged note: He Yan’s own.)

primary.key: The Master said, ‘Learn as if you could not reach your object, and were always fearing also lest you should lose it.’
primary.s: Between a lament over those he does not understand and praise of Shun and Yu, the Master gives a charge on study; He Yan, on 8.17, explains that learning enters from outside and lasts only when thoroughly ripened, hence the fear of losing it.
primary.src: He Yan, Lunyu jijie, on 8.17, zh.wikisource (the Jijie notes in Lunyu zhushu, juan 8), revision 7904524 (2026)

basis.words: 學自外入，至熟乃可長久。如不及，猶恐失之。
basis.gloss: Learning comes in from outside; only when it is thoroughly ripened can it last long. [So one learns] as if not reaching it, and still fears to lose it. (Untagged note: He Yan’s own.)

standby.key: The philosopher Tsang said, ‘The officer may not be without breadth of mind and vigorous endurance. His burden is heavy and his course is long.
standby.s: Before naming perfect virtue the load and death the end, the philosopher Tsang speaks of the officer; Zhu Xi, on 8.7, explains that only breadth bears the weight and only endurance goes the distance, for the resolve may not slacken while breath remains.
standby.src: Zhu Xi, Lunyu jizhu, on 8.7, zh.wikisource (Sishu zhangju jizhu, juan 4), revision 2285801 (2023)

basis.words: 弘，寬廣也。毅，強忍也。非弘不能勝其重，非毅無以致其遠。…一息尚存，此志不容少懈，可謂遠矣。
basis.gloss: Hung is breadth; i is strong endurance. Without breadth one cannot bear its weight; without endurance there is no way to reach its distance. … [On ‘only with death does his course stop’:] while a single breath remains, this resolve may not slacken in the least; this may be called long.

primary.key: The Master said, ‘When the year becomes cold, then we know how the pine and the cypress are the last to lose their leaves.’
primary.s: After praising Tsze-lu’s unashamed poverty, the Master turns to trees in the cold; He Yan, on 9.27, reads it as a figure: in settled times common men also order themselves, and only a muddied age makes the gentleman’s uprightness known.
primary.src: He Yan, Lunyu jijie, on 9.27, zh.wikisource (the Jijie notes in Lunyu zhushu, juan 9), revision 2030329 (2021)

basis.words: 大寒之歲，眾木皆死，然後知松柏小彫傷；平歲則眾木亦有不死者，故須歲寒而後別之。喻凡人處治世亦能自脩整，與君子同；在濁世，然後知君子之正不苟容。
basis.gloss: In a year of great cold all the trees die, and then it is known that the pine and cypress are only a little withered; in an ordinary year many trees also do not die, so it takes a cold year to tell them apart. It is a figure: ordinary men in a well-ordered age can also keep themselves in order, the same as the gentleman; only in a muddied age is the gentleman’s rectitude, which will not stoop to please, known. (Untagged note: He Yan’s own.)

standby.key: The Master standing by a stream, said, ‘It passes on just like this, not ceasing day or night!’
standby.s: Before sayings on an unfinished mound and Hui’s advance, the Master speaks at a river; Zhu Xi, on 9.16, reads it as the ceaseless course of heaven and earth, easiest seen in flowing water, pointed out so learners examine themselves without a moment’s break.
standby.src: Zhu Xi, Lunyu jizhu, on 9.16, zh.wikisource (Sishu zhangju jizhu, juan 5), revision 2018280 (2021)

basis.words: 天地之化，往者過，來者續，無一息之停，乃道體之本然也。然其可指而易見者，莫如川流。故於此發以示人，欲學者時時省察，而無毫髮之間斷也。
basis.gloss: The transformations of heaven and earth, what goes passing and what comes following on, without a breath’s pause: this is the Way’s substance as it is. But of what can be pointed to and easily seen, nothing is like a flowing river. So he spoke of it here to show people, wishing learners to examine themselves at every moment without a hair’s breadth of interruption.

primary.key: The stable being burned down, when he was at court, on his return he said, ‘Has any man been hurt?’ He did not ask about the horses.
primary.s: In a book of his ways at court, at table and at home, a stable burns; Zhu Xi, on 10.12, reads the silence about horses not as indifference but as fear for people leaving no leisure to ask, since principle values people above beasts.
primary.src: Zhu Xi, Lunyu jizhu, on 10.12, zh.wikisource (Sishu zhangju jizhu, juan 5), revision 2018280 (2021)

basis.words: 非不愛馬，然恐傷人之意多，故未暇問。蓋貴人賤畜，理當如此。
basis.gloss: It was not that he did not care for the horses; but his fear that people had been hurt was great, so he had no leisure to ask. For to value people and hold beasts cheap is as principle requires.

standby.key: The Master said, ‘There is the hen-pheasant on the hill bridge. At its season! At its season!’
standby.s: Closing the book, a passage tells of a bird that rises at a look and settles after circling; He Yan, on 10.18, reads the exclamation as a sigh that the hen-pheasant finds its season while man does not find his.
standby.src: He Yan, Lunyu jijie, on 10.18, zh.wikisource (the Jijie notes in Lunyu zhushu, juan 10), revision 2626406 (2025)

basis.words: 言山梁雌雉得其時，而入不得其時，故歎之。
basis.gloss: It means that the hen-pheasant on the hill bridge has found its time, while man has not found his (入 here is the converted text’s slip for 人, man); so he sighed over it. (Untagged note: He Yan’s own.)

primary.key: The Master said, ‘While you are not able to serve men, how can you serve their spirits?’ Chi Lu added, ‘I venture to ask about death?’ He was answered, ‘While you do not know life, how can you know about death?’
primary.s: Chi Lu asks how to serve the spirits of the dead, then about death; He Yan’s collection, on 11.11, gives Chen Qun, who reads them as withholding an answer, since spirits and death are hard to make clear and talk of them profits nothing.
primary.src: He Yan, Lunyu jijie, Chen Qun’s gloss on 11.11, zh.wikisource (the Jijie notes in Lunyu zhushu, juan 11), revision 1375235 (2018)

basis.words: 陳曰：“鬼神及死事難明，語之無益，故不答。”
basis.gloss: Chen Qun (tagged 陳曰 in the collection) says: ‘Spirits and the matter of death are hard to make clear, and speaking of them brings no benefit; so he did not answer.’

standby.key: The Master said, ‘While you are not able to serve men, how can you serve their spirits?’ Chi Lu added, ‘I venture to ask about death?’ He was answered, ‘While you do not know life, how can you know about death?’
standby.s: Chi Lu asks about the spirits of the dead and about death; Zhu Xi, on 11.11, reads the replies as teaching that the hidden and the manifest share one principle, but learning must take them in order, men before spirits and life before death.
standby.src: Zhu Xi, Lunyu jizhu, on 11.11, zh.wikisource (Sishu zhangju jizhu, juan 6), revision 2358541 (2024)

basis.words: 然非誠敬足以事人，則必不能事神；非原始而知所以生，則必不能反終而知所以死。蓋幽明始終，初無二理，但學之有序，不可躐等，故夫子告之如此。
basis.gloss: But without sincerity and reverence enough to serve men, one certainly cannot serve spirits; without tracing back to the beginning and knowing how we come to live, one certainly cannot turn to the end and know how we come to die. For the hidden and the manifest, beginning and end, were never two principles; only learning has its order and may not skip a grade, and so the Master told him thus.

primary.key: The Master said, ‘To subdue one’s self and return to propriety, is perfect virtue.
primary.s: Yen Yuan asks about perfect virtue, and the Master answers, then lists four prohibitions; Zhu Xi, on 12.1, reads the self as the body’s selfish desires and propriety as the ordered pattern of heavenly principle, whose recovery makes the heart’s virtue whole again.
primary.src: Zhu Xi, Lunyu jizhu, on 12.1, zh.wikisource (Sishu zhangju jizhu, juan 6), revision 2358541 (2024)

basis.words: 克，勝也。己，謂身之私慾也。復，反也。禮者，天理之節文也。…故為仁者必有以勝私慾而復於禮，則事皆天理，而本心之德復全於我矣。
basis.gloss: ‘Subdue’ is to overcome. ‘Self’ means the selfish desires of the body. ‘Return’ is to go back. Propriety is the measured pattern of heavenly principle. … So one who practises perfect virtue must overcome selfish desire and return to propriety; then every affair is heavenly principle, and the virtue of the original heart is whole again in him.

standby.key: From of old, death has been the lot of all men; but if the people have no faith in their rulers, there is no standing for the state.
standby.s: Pressed by Tsze-kung, the Master would give up arms and then food before trust; He Yan’s collection, on 12.7, gives Kong Anguo, who reads it as death being common to every age, while one who governs a state may not break faith.
standby.src: He Yan, Lunyu jijie, Kong Anguo’s gloss on 12.7, zh.wikisource (the Jijie notes in Lunyu zhushu, juan 12), revision 2063705 (2021)

basis.words: 孔曰：“死者，古今常道，人皆有之。治邦不可失信。”
basis.gloss: Kong Anguo (tagged 孔曰 in the collection) says: ‘Death is the constant way of past and present; all men have it. One who governs a state may not break faith.’
